content: A set is defined as a collection of distinct objects that are considered as a single entity. Sets are one of the most fundamental concepts in mathematics, and the study of their structure, known as set theory, is a rich and ongoing field of research. Although set theory was only developed at the end of the 19th century, it has become a ubiquitous part of mathematics education and is introduced as early as primary school in many countries. Set theory serves as a foundational framework from which nearly all of mathematics can be derived. Philosophically, sets are often regarded as abstract objects, with their physical representations being, for example, three cups collectively referred to as the cups or the chalk lines on a board forming curly bracket symbols. However, proponents of mathematical realism, such as Penelope Maddy, argue that sets are concrete objects. Georg Cantor, the principal creator of set theory, defined a set as any collection of definite, distinct objects (called elements) that are grouped into a whole. The elements of a set, also referred to as its members, can be anything, such as numbers, people, letters, or even other sets. Sets are conventionally denoted by capital letters. Every element in a set must be unique, meaning no two members can be identical. This property of uniqueness is preserved under all set operations. Additionally, the order in which elements are listed in a set is irrelevant, unlike in sequences or tuples. There are two primary ways to describe or specify the members of a set. The first is by intensional definition, which uses a rule or semantic description to define the set. The second is by extensional definition, which involves listing each member of the set explicitly, enclosed in braces. In an extensional definition, the order of elements and any repetitions are irrelevant. For example, the sets {1, 2, 3} and {3, 2, 1} are equivalent. For sets with many elements, the enumeration of members can be abbreviated using ellipses, which may also be used for sets with infinitely many members. The notation with braces can also be used in an intensional specification, such as E = {playing-card suits}, which represents the set {♠, ♦, ♥, ♣}. A more general form of this is set-builder notation, which allows for the concise representation of sets defined by a rule, such as F = {n² − 4 : n is a whole number from 0 to 19}. In this notation, the colon (:) means such that, and the description specifies the rule for membership in the set. Membership in a set is denoted by the symbol ∈, while non-membership is denoted by ∉. For example, -4 ∈ A and 285 ∈ F (since 285 = 17² − 4), but -9 ∉ F and green ∉ B. The cardinality of a set, denoted |S|, refers to the number of members in the set. For instance, the French flag has three colors, so |B| = 3. The empty set, denoted by the symbol ∅, has no members and a cardinality of zero. For example, the set of all three-sided squares has no members, so its cardinality is 0, and it is equal to the empty set. Despite its apparent simplicity, the empty set is a fundamental concept in mathematics and is essential in axiomatic set theory. Some sets have infinite cardinality, such as the set of natural numbers (N). Furthermore, some infinite cardinalities are larger than others; for example, the set of real numbers has a greater cardinality than the set of natural numbers. Interestingly, the cardinality of the points on a straight line is the same as that of any segment of the line, the entire plane, or any Euclidean space. If every member of set A is also a member of set B, then A is a subset of B, denoted A ⊆ B. Equivalently, B is a superset of A, denoted B ⊇ A. If A is a subset of, but not equal to, B, then A is called a proper subset of B, denoted A ⊂ B. The empty set is a subset of every set, and every set is a subset of itself. For example, the set of all men is a proper subset of the set of all people, and {1, 3} ⊂ {1, 2, 3, 4}. The power set of a set S is the set of all subsets of S, including the empty set and S itself. If S has a finite cardinality n, then its power set has a cardinality of 2ⁿ. For example, the power set of {1, 2, 3} is {{1, 2, 3}, {1, 2}, {1, 3}, {2, 3}, {1}, {2}, {3}, ∅}. The cardinality of the original set is 3, and the cardinality of the power set is 2³ = 8. This relationship is one reason for the term power set. Certain sets hold significant mathematical importance and are frequently referred to by special names and notational conventions. Examples include the set of all primes (ℙ), the set of all natural numbers (ℕ), the set of all whole numbers (ℕ₀), the set of all integers (ℤ), the set of all rational numbers (ℚ), the set of all real numbers (ℝ), and the set of all complex numbers (ℂ). These sets are often represented using blackboard bold typeface. Each of these sets has an infinite number of elements, and they are related by the inclusions ℙ ⊆ ℕ ⊆ ℕ₀ ⊆ ℤ ⊆ ℚ ⊆ ℝ ⊆ ℂ. Basic operations on sets include unions, intersections, complements, and Cartesian products. The union of two sets A and B, denoted A ∪ B, is the set of all elements that are members of either A or B. The intersection of A and B, denoted A ∩ B, is the set of all elements that are members of both A and B. If A ∩ B = ∅, then A and B are disjoint. The relative complement of A in B, denoted B A, is the set of all elements in B that are not in A. The Cartesian product of two sets A and B, denoted A × B, is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) where a ∈ A and b ∈ B. Set theory is foundational to mathematics, as it provides the basis for defining structures in abstract algebra, such as groups, fields, and rings. Relations, which are subsets of Cartesian products, are another important application of set theory. For example, the set of all ordered pairs (x, x²), where x is a real number, represents a familiar mathematical function, f(x) = x². Although naive set theory, which defines a set as any well-defined collection, was initially accepted, it encountered paradoxes such as Russell's paradox and Cantor's paradox. To resolve these issues, set theory was formalized using axiomatic systems based on first-order logic, giving rise to axiomatic set theory. Despite this, naive set theory remains useful for many purposes.
